newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ten bln skr payments may also be tax cuts - Asbrink.
newsitem.headline: Ten bln skr payments may also be tax cuts - Asbrink.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Friday a 10-billion crown ($1.4 billion) budget surplus, which Prime Minister Goran Persson said will go towards social programmes, may also include some tax cuts.

"The measures in 1998 will not consist entirely of payments. Part can be used to reduce tax and cutting employer fees is also a possibility. The measures will be foremost aimed at small- and medium-sized companies," Asbrink said.
Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said this week he would use a 10-billion crown budget surplus forecast for 1998 on education, health care, care for the elderly and day care.
Later, he said this would not be a one-off payment, but would remain over the coming years.
Asbrink said much needed to be done before it was established exactly how the money would be allocated. The final plan would be mapped out in the spring budget due in April.
"All the measures have a strong connection to employment," Asbrink said.

Asbrink also said the economy was developing more favourably than expected and that 1996's budget deficit would be just above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) compared to an earlier forecast of four percent.

"The development has been more favourable than we had estimated in the autumn. In September, we forecast a budget deficit for 1996 of about four percent. Now, we see it will be just over three percent," Asbrink said.
Asbrink repeated the government's budget goals.
"This means that there will be a budget deficit below three percent in 1997 and this, we will reach with a wide margin.
"In 1998, we will have a balanced budget and the third goal is a budget surplus after 1998, meaning 1999 and thereafter. We have not changed, weakened or postponed this goal," he said.
Since the plan was announced, Swedish debt yields have risen and the crown has weakened in the past few days. But he said he was not worried about the market reaction.
"I am not concerned about the development on particular days. The trend in the Swedish economy is what the market should look at. The development is in an unequivocally postive direction," he said.
-- Henrik Alberius, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1250 ($ = 7.227 Swedish Crowns)
